title: On 4 May, Trump Said the Reflecting Pool Coating Was So Strong 'You Can't Even Cut It' With a Knife. On 22 June, He Said Vandals Cut a '350-Foot Slit' in the Pool Bottom. The Bulwark Published the Side-by-Side. Reporters Could Not Find the Slit (22 June 2026)
narrative:
On Monday 22 June 2026, President Donald Trump escalated his explanation for why the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is plagued by peeling paint and algae blooms, claiming without evidence that 'vandals' used a knife or box cutter to slash a '350-foot slit' in the bottom of the pool between the World War II Memorial and the Lincoln Memorial. Trump told reporters that the National Park Service had arrested five people and had five more under investigation, and that 'they cut it, they cut it very violently. The same thing with the floor, they cut it, and then they lifted it. They pulled it, and that's what it is.' When pressed by CBS News senior White House correspondent Ed O'Keefe for proof — photos or video of the alleged slit — Trump responded that proof would emerge 'in court' and that reporters could verify by calling the Department of Interior or the Parks Department.

On Monday night Trump went further on Truth Social, writing that 'we are preparing lawsuits against ABC for false reporting' over its coverage of the pool's condition, and claiming his two predecessors spent '$100 million' on the Reflecting Pool renovation — a figure that does not match the public record. The Obama administration spent approximately $35 million on the pool. The Biden administration oversaw no major work on the pool. The recent Trump-era renovation cost approximately $14.7 million, the figure most often cited in contemporaneous reporting. Trump also suggested that 'somebody said they might have put fertilizer' in the pool to cause the algae, again without providing evidence.

The contradiction at the heart of the story: on 4 May 2026, in on-camera remarks about the same renovation, Trump described the pool's coating as essentially indestructible. 'This will last for at least 50 years, you'll never have a leak. It's very strong,' Trump said on 4 May. 'You couldn't, if you had a knife. I don't want to give anybody ideas. If you had a knife, you can't even cut it. So strong, so powerful. It's like powerful rubber.' The Bulwark posted a side-by-side video comparison of the two statements on 22 June. ABC News Chief Washington Correspondent Jonathan Karl, reporting from the pool last week, reached down and held up a piece of peeling paint that was still connected to the bottom so viewers could see what was happening — the visible evidence on which Trump's response accused Karl of 'trying to rip the rubber off of the surface.'

analysis:
The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool story is a documentary-credibility piece about a temporal contradiction paired with a deflection pattern, not a piece about vandalism. The pattern is structurally identical to the July 2024 'they're eating the dogs' Springfield episode, the August 2024 'they took the funding' hurricane-relief episode, and the September 2024 'she had the rally-sized crowd' debate episode: an on-camera claim that is testable in the open record (the 4 May statement), followed by a contradictory later claim (the 22 June '350-foot slit'), followed by third-party evidentiary deferral (the Department of Interior / Parks Department), followed by a litigation threat against the reporter who demonstrated the defect (ABC News).

The temporal contradiction is the load-bearing finding. The 4 May on-camera statement that 'you can't even cut it' with a knife is the primary documentary record of Trump's earlier claim that the coating was knife-resistant. The Bulwark posted the side-by-side comparison on 22 June; HuffPost's reporting cites both timestamps verbatim. The temporal gap (4 May → 22 June, approximately seven weeks) is short enough that the contradiction cannot be attributed to a change in product or contractor — it is the same coating, the same contractor, the same site. The contradiction is in Trump's claim about the coating, not in the coating itself.

The '350-foot slit' is the kind of claim that is testable in two independent ways. CBS's Ed O'Keefe explicitly told Trump that 'reporters who visited the site found no evidence of such damage.' Trump's response — 'Well, you'd have to go see the Parks Department. They'll show it to you, or see, see the secretary, but I saw it' — is the canonical deflection: the alleged evidence exists but is held by a third party the reporter has not contacted. The U.S. Park Police confirmed five arrests for vandalism related to the Reflecting Pool and five additional federal citations, but 'neither the company behind the project nor the U.S. Park Service has said a cut slit was responsible for the peeling.' The arrest count is real; the connection between the arrests and the alleged 350-foot slit is unsupported by any official statement.

The 'I saw it' claim has no supporting photographic record. ABC News's Jonathan Karl reached down and held up a piece of peeling paint that was still connected to the pool bottom — visual evidence of peeling, not slashing. Trump's claim that Karl was 'trying to rip the rubber off of the surface' reframes the act of demonstrating a defect as the cause of the defect. This is a different documentary-credibility pattern from the 4 May / 22 June temporal contradiction: it is the in-real-time falsification of a present-tense claim by the act of on-camera reporting.

The dollar-figure inflation is the secondary finding. Trump's 22 June Truth Social post claimed Obama and Biden spent 'over 100 Million Dollars on the Reflecting Pool.' Mediaite's reporting confirms: 'President Joe Biden oversaw no major work on it. Meanwhile, the Obama administration spent $35 million on the pool.' Trump's own recent renovation cost approximately $14.7 million — a number he appears to have inflated by an order of magnitude in the same Truth Social post that threatened ABC with a lawsuit. The Truth Social post also said 'I spent approximately 16 Million Dollars' — higher than the documented $14.7 million contract value. The combined effect is that a Truth Social post threatening litigation against ABC for 'false reporting' contained two self-inflating dollar figures (predecessors: $100M, self: $16M) on a topic where public records exist.

The 'fertilizer in the pool' algae claim closes the credibility circle. Trump's 22 June claim that 'somebody said they might have put fertilizer, they did something to create the algae' is sourced to no identifiable official or expert. 'Somebody said' is the entire evidentiary chain. The algae bloom is documented; the fertilizer-introduction mechanism is not. It is the same documentary posture as the slit: a claim is made, the claim is testable, and the source for the claim is held by an unnamed third party that has not been produced.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: On 22 June 2026, President Trump claimed that vandals cut a '350-foot slit' in the bottom of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool — a facility whose coating he had described on 4 May as so strong 'you can't even cut it' with a knife. The Bulwark posted a side-by-side video of the two statements on 22 June. CBS News's Ed O'Keefe told Trump reporters who visited the site found no evidence of such damage; Trump deflected to the Department of Interior and the Parks Department. U.S. Park Police confirmed five arrests and five additional federal citations, but 'neither the company behind the project nor the U.S. Park Service has said a cut slit was responsible for the peeling.' ABC News's Jonathan Karl demonstrated the peeling paint on-camera; Trump accused him of 'trying to rip the rubber off of the surface.' Trump's Truth Social post claimed predecessors spent '$100 million' on the pool (public record: Obama $35M, Biden none) and that he spent 'approximately 16 Million Dollars' (public record: ~$14.7M). The story is a case study in on-camera self-contradiction (the 4 May → 22 June temporal contradiction), third-party evidentiary deferral (Department of Interior / Parks Department), and litigation threat against the reporter who showed the defect (ABC News).
